lines.text: Great programmers plan before they type. Today you plan a quiz game with AI, then build it yourself.
Write your idea in one sentence, like a three-question quiz about India that keeps score.
Say who will play it and what counts as winning.
A clear idea makes a clear plan.
Pseudocode is your program written as plain English steps.
Each step is one small action, like ask a question or add one to the score.
It is not Python yet, so anyone can read it.
Ask the AI to review your steps or suggest a plan in pseudocode only.
Tell it not to write the code.
Then check the plan for missing steps before you build.
Turn one step into code, run it, and only then add the next step.
Test with right answers, wrong answers and capital letters.
The code is yours, because you built every line.
Zoya asks for a plan in pseudocode only, and the AI keeps to that rule.
The plan looks tidy, but trace it with your finger: when does the score go up?
It never does, so every player would score zero. Zoya adds the missing step.
Zoya turns each pseudocode step into one or two lines of Python.
She uses lower so that Delhi with a capital letter still counts as correct.
She runs it after every question, not just at the very end.
You can build the same plan in Scratch with ask and wait, and an if else block.
The plan is the same in any language, only the code looks different.
Test your game the way a real player might use it, including the silly ways.
Every test that fails is a new bug to hunt, using your debug loop from last lesson.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
